chapter: Radio, theaters and early dance forms
title: Jazz in the Palace pit and young Santo Pecora
summary: DeDroit says his muted playing made jazz a feature at the Palace, and recalls trombonist Santo Pecora playing with him at seventeen.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Now, now, I took you off from the theater, which was strictly long here, until I went in there, and when I started playing that Charno We Own A Lot To You, with the mute, the house came down, it became a feature. So the Palace had to do the same thing. And they had better jazz men than we had, and Melvin Berry, who was my trombonist tonight. You see, the boys used to double. Now, Santa Picora, was my, when Berry went to California, Berry got a big job out there. Santo came in my band. Santa Picora, you know him, don't you? I met him. Interviewed him in November. He played with me when he was only seventeen. When we went at the tuxedo, he came with a pink great machine shirt on, but he wants to kill me when I tell that to people. It's the truth. He didn't know that. His father was a tailor, he should have known better. But that band used to dress. Oh boy, I would dress when it was good for me to look good. But Santo was playing an act at the Palace one time and the man said to the leader, he says, you know, the trombone play, he's not playing my music. And the leader said, I think it was Fulco at the time, he says, you know, he's a great jazz man, and he never makes, the guy said, don't apologize for him. He says, he plays it better than my music. You know? So jazz took a hold of the orphanage to such an extent that I used to have to stand up in the pit and bow with the axe.
